How World War Heroes merged 100m+ player accounts and reshaped matchmaking
Last Level Games developer Mikhail Orlov explains how the studio merged its iOS and Android databases and the unexpected impact on matchmaking

Last Level Games migrated more than 100 million World War Heroes player accounts across iOS and Android into a shared server.
The larger player pool improved matchmaking quality but initially reduced player satisfaction as players faced more real opponents instead of bots.

We migrated over 100 million World War Heroes player accounts from two separate game platforms - iOS and Android - into a single shared server. The databases had overlapping IDs in every table, and the social graph meant we couldn't move users one by one. We needed under two hours of planned downtime, the ability to roll back, and a way for QA to test on real production data before release.
This article covers how we solved it using Postgres logical replication with a custom middleware layer that transforms data on the wire. You'll see how we handled the ID offset scheme across regions, the business logic edge cases we didn't expect, and what went wrong on release night, and how the merge unexpectedly changed matchmaking quality.
The problem
Background:
Our game, WWH, runs on both iOS and Android. For historical reasons, these two platforms always had completely separate backend infrastructure - separate servers, separate databases, separate everything. At some point we decided to merge both platforms into a single server with one shared player pool.
Each platform had 11 databases per region, with game data on the main cluster and statistics on a separate one. Three regions: EU, NA and AS. Around 50 tables total per platform. Total data volume: 4.8 TB on the largest EU server alone, over 9 TB combined. Everything ran on Postgres 13.
QA needs to test the merged result on real production data before players see it.
Every entity in every table on both platforms had overlapping primary keys. User ID 1 on iOS is a different person than user ID 1 on Android, and the same goes for clan IDs, item IDs, weapon IDs, transaction IDs - everything. You can't just dump one platform's data into the other.
Beyond the raw ID conflicts, users could register via Facebook, and the same Facebook account might exist on both platforms. Players have social connections - friendships, clan memberships, in-game mail, chat history. You can't migrate users in isolation without breaking the social graph.
Hard constraints:
Maximum 1-2 hours of downtime
Rollback must remain possible if something breaks at release
QA needs to test the merged result on real production data before players see it
What we considered
Background migration at login. Shift data gradually as users authenticate. Minimal downtime in theory, but the implementation complexity is high. No clean rollback, no way to test on production data, and any data bug affects live users immediately.
Real-time migration at cutover. After a predefined cutoff time, migrate user's entire datasets on login. Same problems: no rollback, no pre-testing, and this approach dumps heavy migration work onto the system at exactly the moment when login traffic is highest.
What Postgres doesn't give you is data transformation in transit.
Script-based background migration. A process runs continuously, migrating users in the background. More controllable - rollback is possible by simply not switching traffic, and you can test the target database. But now you need custom infrastructure to track migration state across 11 databases, handle partial failures, retries, and crash recovery reliably - for a process that has to run for potentially weeks on live data.
Debezium. A solid CDC tool built on top of Postgres logical replication. It captures changes and streams them to Kafka. But for our use case, it would bring significant operational overhead: a JVM service and a Kafka cluster to run and monitor.
Transformation logic would have to be implemented separately from the replication setup. And ultimately Debezium is designed for general-purpose event streaming, not for a one-time migration with complex custom transformation rules defined per column in a known fixed schema.
None of these felt like the right fit.
The approach
The right foundation:
Logical replication
works at the row level using a publish/subscribe model. You create a publication on the source listing which tables to expose, and a subscription on the target that connects to it. The subscriber receives the current data snapshot, then a continuous stream of changes.
What Postgres doesn't give you is data transformation in transit. User ID 1 arrives as user ID 1.
So we built a thin middleware layer that sits between publisher and subscriber and rewrites data on the wire. Postgres handles every hard part. The middleware handles only the transformation.
ID offset strategy
The core transformation is simple: add a fixed offset to every ID and every foreign key reference to that ID.
Every entity had to be modified - not just users and clans, but weapons, items, inventory entries, transactions, battle logs, notifications, mail - anything with a primary key and everything that referenced those keys. Across ~50 tables per platform, the config covered all of it.
Rather than picking arbitrary offsets, we designed them to be useful beyond this migration. We might eventually want to merge regional servers (EU, NA, AS) into a single global server. If each region's data lands in a non-overlapping numeric range, a future regional merge would require only standard logical replication - no middleware, no transformation. So the offsets we
